summary: The note describes the Mandate of Heaven (Tian Ming), a Chinese political and religious doctrine used since ancient times to justify imperial rule. It explains that Heaven bestows the mandate on a just ruler, that a dynasty's overthrow signaled lost virtue, and that natural disasters were read as signs of Heaven's displeasure. It traces the doctrine from its first use by the Zhou kings against the Shang, through later dynasties including the Qing, to neighboring Korea and Vietnam. The note also includes some loosely argued claims, such as that the peasantry were the real selectors under the Ming and that the doctrine ended with the founding of the People's Republic of China.
one_line: A Chinese political and religious doctrine holding that Heaven grants rule to a just emperor, first used by the Zhou to justify overthrowing the Shang.
key_facts: The Mandate of Heaven, or Tian Ming (Chinese: 天命; pinyin: Tiānmìng), is a Chinese political and religious doctrine used since ancient times to justify the rule of the Emperor of China.
According to the doctrine, heaven (天, Tian) embodies the natural order and will of the universe and bestows the mandate on a just ruler of China, the 'Heavenly Son' of the 'Celestial Empire'.
If a ruler was overthrown, this was interpreted as an indication that the ruler was unworthy and had lost the mandate.
It was a common belief that natural disasters such as famine and flood were signs of heaven's displeasure with the ruler, so revolts often followed major disasters.

The concept of the Mandate of Heaven was first used to support the rule of the kings of the Zhou dynasty (1046 -- 256 BCE) and legitimize their overthrow of the earlier Shang dynasty (1600 -- 1069 BCE).
Rebellion against the Shang was led by Zhou Wu, and the Zhou believed the Shang ruling house had become morally corrupt and lost its virtue.
The Shang dynasty was ruled by 31 kings over 17 generations, and its rulers' abuse of other social classes led to social unrest and instability.
The doctrine was used throughout Chinese history to legitimize the overthrow and installation of new emperors, including non-Han ethnic monarchs such as the Qing dynasty (1636 -- 1912).
Qing emperors took their advisors' feedback very seriously and reflected on their decisions when natural disasters occurred.
The note states that the doctrine was also used by monarchs in neighboring countries such as Korea and Vietnam.
According to the note, the peasant group of the Ming dynasty were the real selectors who allowed the Mandate of Heaven to be claimed by the ruler.

Towards the end of the Qing dynasty, as the Peoples Republic of China began to be established, there was no more Mandate to be claimed, and the note states there was no formal statement or writing of the Mandate of Heaven.
